The foundational structure of human development is modeled as a sequence of discrete interest phases governed by entropy and habit formation. Each phase represents a stochastic process where initial conditions (habits, environment) determine long-term behavioral outcomes. The system exhibits phase transitions driven by time-dependent entropy loss, leading to saturation points where interest wanes. This framework supports a dualism between internal motivation and external influence, where early habits act as priors shaping later passions. The model assumes that each interest domain has a finite lifetime before transitioning to the next, with entropy as the primary driver of decay. Failure modes include premature entropy exhaustion, lack of environmental reinforcement, and absence of early habit formation. These transitions are not linear but governed by non-equilibrium thermodynamics of attention and engagement, where the system seeks equilibrium through repeated cycles of exploration and fixation.
